stories.primary_headline: 'They made me give my shirt to another actor': 'Mandaadi' actor Soori recounts shocking humiliation by Tamil star

primary_source.headline: 'They made me give my shirt to another actor': 'Mandaadi' actor Soori recounts shocking humiliation by Tamil star
primary_source.content:
Kollywood actor Soori, who started off his career as a comedian and emerged as a leading actor in Tamil cinema, is eagerly awaiting the release of his much-talked-about movie Mandaadi. During the promotions of the movie, the actor looked back on the harsh realities of his early days in the film industry.Opening up about a painful past experience, the actor recalled a heartbreaking moment when a top star replaced him with an actor who had arrived via a reference. Making matters worse, the crew took his personal shirt and gave it to the replacement actor, never bothering to ask his consent or return it.'Is rape end of a woman's life': Swara Bhasker defends letter to Sanjay Leela Bhansali on 'Padmaavat' jauhar scene "I had shot my scenes alongside a major comedian and a leading superstar. I thought it was my big breakthrough. But after reviewing the shot on the monitor, the hero and the director spoke in private, and everything changed in an instant," said Soori.pic.twitter.com/rmzVwlLvB0&mdash; Amuthabharathi Videos (@videos3210) September 1, 2026
 

"They asked me to take off my shirt so the new actor could wear it. My shirt was tossed into the costume vehicle, and I was left standing on set in just a towel wrapped around my waist, searching for my clothes while they filmed the scene with someone else," Soori added.He further looked back on the hardships of his early career. The actor opened up about a defining, vulnerable moment when he was on the verge of his first major break, only for the opportunity to be snatched away under humiliating conditions.        View this post on Instagram            
 Soori also revealed that the incident caused him immense pain and humiliation at the time but became a major turning point. The setback only hardened his determination to make it in the industry purely on merit, rather than relying on favours or connections, he said.Social media is pouring out love for Soori following his raw revelation during the Mandaadi promotions. Fans are celebrating his remarkable journey, hailing his impressive performances in powerhouse films like Garudan, Kottukkaali, and Vetrimaaran’s two-part saga Viduthalai.

stories.primary_headline: 'My best film yet': Emraan Hashmi on 'Awarapan 2' success

primary_source.headline: 'My best film yet': Emraan Hashmi on 'Awarapan 2' success
primary_source.content:
Riding high on the success of his latest release, Awarapan 2, actor Emraan Hashmi has called the action-emotional thriller his "best film yet." Talking about the journey of reviving the iconic character Shivam Pandit nearly two decades after the original, Emraan credited producer Vishesh Bhatt’s relentless persistence and vision for breathing new life into the franchise.The sequel, which released in theaters on August 14, 2026, has turned into a major box office juggernaut, minting over Rs 200 crore globally. For Emraan, the success represents personal redemption for the 2007 cult classic Awarapan, which gained massive popularity on home video and television over the years despite performing averagely during its initial theatrical release.'Awarapan 2' Box Office: Emraan Hashmi starrer crosses Rs 128 crore on Day 7, eyes big second weekendLooking back on the film’s warm reception, Emraan wrote on Instagram:"I’ve always held Shivam Pandit very close to my heart. When Vishesh came to me with the idea for Awarapan 2, I was hesitant because sequels to beloved cult films carry huge expectations. But Vishesh had a singular, clear vision—he didn't just want to make a cash grab; he wanted to give Shivam the emotional closure and grand scale he deserved. Looking at how audiences have embraced the film, I can confidently say it’s my best work to date."        View this post on Instagram            
 Emraan concluded his note with an appeal to audiences. He urged viewers to experience Awarapan 2 on the big screen: “Feel the emotional roller coaster. Let the music take over. And celebrate it the way it was meant to be celebrated - a big screen, big sound cinematic experience.”Earlier, producer Vishesh Bhatt revealed that convincing Emraan to step back into the role took time, as the actor was initially cautious about revisiting the broken anti-hero nearly 19 years later."Emraan and I both carried the heartache of Awarapan not getting its financial due back in 2007," Vishesh Bhatt shared.        View this post on Instagram            
 'Awarapan 2' movie review: When nostalgia isn't enoughFrom Emraan Hashmi to Ajay Devgn: When Bollywood’s villains were broken men, not killing machines "There was a strong spiritual core to Shivam’s character that felt incomplete. I knew we had to honour those silences and emotional depth while adapting to modern cinema standards. Once Emraan saw the script by Bilal Siddiqui and Nitin Kakkar, everything clicked," he added.Directed by Nitin Kakkar, Awarapan 2 follows an older, retired Shivam Pandit who is drawn out of isolation and into Bangkok’s dangerous underbelly to bust a child trafficking network. Aptly supported by hit music and high-octane action sequences, the film has delivered one of the biggest box office comebacks of Emraan Hashmi’s career.During a recent theater visit, interacting with fans, Hashmi teased that given the overwhelming audience demand, discussions for a potential Awarapan 3 may already be on the horizon.

stories.primary_headline: A$AP Rocky review – arena spectacular has plenty of helicopters but little sense of direction

primary_source.headline: A$AP Rocky review – arena spectacular has plenty of helicopters but little sense of direction
primary_source.content: O2 Arena, LondonThe polymath rapper’s stage show, which also features SWAT teams and a warship, is truly bravura stuff – but you can’t help feeling this is an artist at a creative crossroadsA$AP Rocky dangles precariously from a helicopter, while beneath him black-clad SWAT officers brawl with his white-masked followers. This isn’t some cliffhanger setpiece from the rapper/actor’s latest film – it’s just how shows on his Don’t Be Dumb tour open. It’s a big production: there are further prop helicopters, including a smaller one up in the rafters from which he also raps (a reference to his single Helicopter), while the stage recreates the top deck of a naval warship, for reasons that never become clear.The bizarre set underscores a sense of a man in career transition, unsure who he is any more. In the eight years since his last album, this survivor of homelessness and incarceration became a father, three times, with Rihanna; he’s pivoting towards movies – good ones – and co-chairs the Met Gala. His new record sought to redefine him as an artist, juggling more of his trademark pugilistic rap with ambitious stylistic experiments and unexpected collaborations (Damon Albarn! Danny Elfman!). stories.primary_headline: A 12TB Steam "teraleak" spills more than a decade of lost PC gaming history

primary_source.headline: A 12TB Steam “teraleak” spills more than a decade of lost PC gaming history
primary_source.content:
Here at Ars, we're intimately familiar with data leaks surrounding Valve's games, hardware, and the workings of Steam itself. But nothing could have prepared us for this weekend's "terarelease" encompassing more than 12TB of content related to seemingly every title available on Steam between 2003 and 2013.
What's being sold as an "as-complete-as-possible ... content server dump" of Steam's defunct "Steam2" server architecture from that time period is now circulating around via a BitTorrent tracker that Valve seems unlikely to ever completely purge from the Internet. The massive collection includes thousands of "depots" representing what seems to be every version of every game uploaded to those old Steam2 servers. That includes public release builds, of course, but in many cases also covers previously unseen pre-release, prototype, and playtest versions of popular titles published by Valve and third-party Steam publishers.
Steam2: Electric Boogaloo
The reason this weekend's leaked content cuts off abruptly in 2013 is because that's when Valve updated its content distribution system from "Steam2" to the current SteamPipe system. In moving from a proprietary file distribution format to standard HTTP file trees, the new system removed various update approval bottlenecks on Valve's end and streamlined update and patch downloads so they only reflected file differentials.Read full article

primary_source.headline: Waking Life: Richard Linklater’s genre-defying indie is a kaleidoscopic masterpiece
primary_source.content: Wiley Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, whose reality-bending encounters make him uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep“I’m gonna tell you about a dream I once had,” Richard Linklater – playing himself in his own film Waking Life – tells Wiley Wiggins, playing the film’s unnamed protagonist. “I know when someone says that usually you’re in for a very boring next few minutes, and you might be,” Linklater adds as he hammers away at a pinball machine. “But it sounds like … what else you gonna do, right?”On paper, that’s the premise – and, if you’re cynical, the central dilemma – of Linklater’s 2001 genre-defying indie masterpiece. Wiggins plays a man wandering around Austin, Texas, who is uncertain whether he’s awake or asleep. He may be stuck in a dream, unable to wake up – or reality might just be this weird. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: 'Not just Hollywood crap': Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK

primary_source.headline: ‘Not just Hollywood crap’: Mike Leigh on the East End communist who brought world cinema to the UK
primary_source.content: A new season at the BFI celebrates Contemporary Films and its founder Charles Cooper, who bet on Britain taking to Ingmar Bergman, Yasujiro Ozu, Stayajjit Ray – and a young Mike LeighOccasionally, vital pieces of the cultural jigsaw disappear without anyone really noticing. This, sadly, was the fate of Contemporary Films, the British film distributor that popularised sophisticated, grownup international cinema – foreign language mostly – in the UK, and heralded the arrival of the auteur generation with directors such as Ingmar Bergman, Satyajit Ray, Andrzej Wajda and Yasujiro Ozu.Contemporary, and its founder Charles Cooper, weren’t the only game in town – Kenneth Rive’s Gala was a fellow traveller – but Contemporary got there first, setting up shop in 1951, first with short films for the then popular film society sector, and moving into features with the 1952 Japanese film Children of Hiroshima. Its marketplace clout faded rapidly in the early 1990s, when it was a victim of changing industry practices. But amazingly, the company is still with us – and is planning a 75th anniversary series of screenings to showcase its history. Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: 'Get up, get breakfast, noise': the teen going viral for enduring all 400 of Merzbow's ear-splitting albums

primary_source.headline: ‘Get up, get breakfast, noise’: the teen going viral for enduring all 400 of Merzbow’s ear-splitting albums
primary_source.content: The infamous Japanese noise artist has a vast and forbidding catalogue that commands a cult fandom. Sam Andrews, 18, is vlogging his way through the lot – and taking a stand for deep listeningAn Instagram Reel that looks like an 80s coming-of-age movie pops up on your feed. It’s four teenage boys in an American-style basement – comfy sofas, guitars, ping pong table – jeering and laughing. But they aren’t secretly drinking beer or planning on sneaking out. They’re brandishing a vinyl copy of Pulse Demon, the most popular album from the cult Japanese noise artist Merzbow, and subjecting themselves to its brutally harsh sound in full, for fun. “I think this is the Book of Revelation: The Soundtrack,” one guy blurts out, a vague look of fear in his eyes.Merzbow, real name Masami Akita, is the world’s most renowned noise artist. Since 1979, Akita has released more than 400 recordings, which range from a 10-hour long album misleadingly titled Merzbient (it’s anything but ambient) to a free-noise supergroup called Flying Testicle. Since February, Sam Andrews, the video’s 18-year-old creator, has been attempting to listen to every one, and is documenting his progress online each day. “I think of my day in album-size chunks,” he says, laughing. “It’s like, get up at seven, get breakfast and then headphones in: noise.” Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: 'it's more freaky, more balls to the wall': how alt-country won over a new generation

primary_source.headline: ‘It’s more freaky, more balls to the wall’: how alt-country won over a new generation
primary_source.content: From Waxahatchee and Florry in the US to Brown Horse and Little Grandad in the UK, a wave of young songwriters are reinvigorating the subgenre’s earnest emotion and twang‘It’s so important to talk about this before it’s gone,” says Francie Medosch, singer, guitarist and songwriter of the band Florry, “because it’s really a flash in the pan.” The flash she means is a brief moment where it feels as though on both sides of the Atlantic, scores of exciting indie bands are playing something that, without slavish copying, has plainly drawn inspiration from alt-country, the music that emerged in the US in the late 1980s and early 90s, when former punks such as Uncle Tupelo – featuring future Wilco co-founder Jeff Tweedy – and the Bottle Rockets picked up picked up fiddles, banjos and acoustic guitars.In the UK, Brown Horse and Vegas Water Taxi have the weeping pedal steel, in the former case tied to something very heartland and in the latter paired with a very English indie sensibility. Westside Cowboy and Little Grandad both borrow from the spiky rootsiness of early Wilco, while Wyatt play slacker country rock. Over in the US, where there’s always going to be more of this sort of thing, you can point to the current indie-rock holy trinity of Waxahatchee, Wednesday and MJ Lenderman, plus Florry, Ratboys, Thomas Dollbaum, Fust, SG Goodman, Lily Seabird, Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band and more. Continue reading...

It provided some relief for audiences, but even more so for the industry at large, with the season pushing past the magic $4bn mark to become the biggest since 2019, up 20% from last year. There were the expected hits (Spider-Man never misses), but there were also unprecedented breakouts (we were obsessed with Obsession) and surprise underperformers (are kids Minions-ed out?)So at the end of a season with epic highs and cavernous lows, what lessons can Hollywood learn? stories.primary_headline: The Extractor review – Indonesian hostage-rescue thriller has surprising thread of gentleness at its core

primary_source.headline: The Extractor review – Indonesian hostage-rescue thriller has surprising thread of gentleness at its core
primary_source.content: Iko Uwais directs and acts in the story of a band of elite soldiers who must rescue a group of researchers taken captive in the jungleCan an elite team of soldiers rescue a band of innocent hostages from a bunch of mean old terrorists? Yes, probably, since there are few (if any) action movies in which the hostages are wiped out and the terrorists win. Not to be confused with the Extraction action franchise starring Chris Hemsworth as a mercenary named Tyler, nor with action thriller Escape Plan: The Extractors, starring Dave Bautista as a prison security expert named Trent, this is an Indonesian action thriller in which actor/director Iko Uwais plays a soldier named Timur. The film was actually called Timur originally, but there’s no denying that The Extractor is a more commercial title (unless you are particularly interested in the medieval Mongol khanates) and will attract more viewers to this tale of hostages, heroes and long-ago childhood friends.In some ways, though, the rebrand is a shame, because the new title suggests the film is more generic than it is. While the basic plot, in which a bunch of researchers are taken hostage in the jungle by an armed group of wrong ’uns, is hardly unique, there are sequences in the film that stand out from the direct-to-video action content mill. In Indonesia, timur means “east”, where the sun rises, and it carries the connotation of hopefulness. That softer feeling in the original title is a key part of the film’s identity, which includes sentimental flashbacks to the childhoods of various characters whose lives have taken tragically different paths. (Can you imagine a world in which a terrorist and a soldier knew each other as children? The Extractor can.) Continue reading...

stories.primary_headline: Pin de Fartie review – spoonerist remix of Samuel Beckett's Endgame finds fresh absurdity in Argentina

primary_source.headline: Pin de Fartie review – spoonerist remix of Samuel Beckett’s Endgame finds fresh absurdity in Argentina
primary_source.content: Beckett’s masterpiece is given a postmodern cinema slant, with characters in different locations, music and humour in a free and fanciful interpretationRemember remixes? Where you take a song and swap out parts of it with new or pre-existing material, changing it just enough to be still recognisable? Argentinean director Alejo Moguillansky applies this quintessentially postmodern aesthetic to film with a funky cinematic remix, or even series of remixes, of Samuel Beckett’s one-act play Fin de Partie, AKA Endgame. The result feels a little retro and possibly a bit too pleased with its own cleverness, and the spoonerist title is juvenile. But in the end this really achieves something with both the source material and the remix that’s fresh, pleasingly provocative, and at times moving.Beckett’s 1957 absurdist masterwork has just four characters on stage throughout, two of whom do most of the talking: cantankerous blind, disabled Hamm banters with his servant/slave Clov, while Hamm’s parents, Nagg and Nell, live in dustbins upstage and talk rather less. There’s an air of apocalyptic doom, much talk of drugs, food and, above all, time running out. Continue reading...
